mechanism_narrative: A sustained increase in the federal funds rate over the preceding three months signals a tightening monetary policy stance, raising discount rates and reducing present value of future corporate cash flows, thus driving negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 trading days.
candidate_trigger: FEDFUNDS rises by >0.5% q/q over last 3 months
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are positive in more than 60% of triggered episodes, or the median return is not statistically different from zero at 5% significance.

mechanism_narrative: A year-over-year decline in real personal consumption expenditures (proxied by GDPC1) signals weakening aggregate demand, which reduces corporate earnings expectations and leads to lower S&P 500 returns over the subsequent 60 trading days.
failure_condition: S&P 500 posts positive 60-day forward returns in more than 70% of triggered episodes, or the average return exceeds +1%.

mechanism_narrative: A persistent rise in the unemployment rate above 6% for two consecutive months signals deteriorating labor market conditions, which depresses consumer spending and corporate margins, resulting in negative S&P 500 returns over the next 20 trading days.
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are positive in more than 50% of triggered months, or the median return is not statistically below zero at 5% significance.

mechanism_narrative: A sustained month-over-month contraction in industrial production (INDPRO) below -0.5% signals supply-side stress, which raises input costs and reduces output, leading to negative S&P 500 returns over the next 20 trading days.
candidate_trigger: INDPRO m/m change < -0.5% for 2 consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are positive in more than 55% of triggered episodes, or the mean return is not statistically different from zero at 5% significance.

mechanism_narrative: A co-movement between real personal consumption expenditures (GDPC1) and housing starts (HOUST) both falling for three consecutive months indicates synchronized weakness in major demand components, which reduces earnings growth and causes negative S&P 500 returns over the next 60 trading days.
candidate_trigger: GDPC1 and HOUST both decline m/m for 3 consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 60-day forward returns are positive in more than 50% of triggered periods, or the average return is not statistically below zero at 5% significance.

mechanism_narrative: When the federal funds rate is above 5% and CPI inflation (CPIAUCSL) is rising above 2% for three consecutive months, the combination signals a high policy rate in an inflationary environment, which erodes real corporate earnings and triggers negative S&P 500 returns over the next 60 trading days.
candidate_trigger: FEDFUNDS > 5% AND CPIAUCSL y/y change > 2% for 3 consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 60-day forward returns are positive in more than 50% of triggered regimes, or the median return is not statistically below zero at 5% significance.

mechanism_narrative: A sharp acceleration in payroll employment (PAYEMS) growth above +0.5% m/m for two consecutive months signals a tight labor market, which boosts wage pressures and input costs, ultimately resulting in positive S&P 500 returns over the next 20 trading days due to higher profit margins in some sectors.
candidate_trigger: PAYEMS m/m change > 0.5% for 2 consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are negative in more than 60% of triggered episodes, or the median return is not statistically above zero at 5% significance.

mechanism_narrative: A persistent rise in real retail sales (RSAFS) above +0.5% m/m for four consecutive months signals improving consumer demand, which boosts corporate revenue and earnings expectations, leading to positive S&P 500 returns over the next 20 trading days regardless of regime.
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are negative in more than 55% of triggered months, or the average return is not statistically above zero at 5% significance.
